headline: Trump, Xi and Putin’s New World Order

paragraphs.text: President Trump left a summit in China with no deal for the American people but lots of love for Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. In this episode, the Opinion writer Michelle Cottle talks to the columnists Jamelle Bouie and David French about Trump’s affection for autocracy, the hubris of A.I. power players — like Nvidia’s former chief executive, Jensen Huang — and how Democrats plan to go after corruption in the new term.

Below is a transcript of an episode of “The Opinions.” We recommend listening to it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the player above or on the NYTimes app, Apple, Spotify, Amazon Music, YouTube, iHeartRadio or wherever you get your podcasts.
The transcript has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Michelle Cottle: So today, which is Thursday for us, Donald Trump held the U.S.’s first ever trilateral summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir V. Putin. Ahead of the meeting, the president had said he wanted to discuss nuclear nonproliferation, along with the wars in Ukraine and Iran. At the end of the day, there were no major diplomatic breakthroughs, although Trump did greet Putin with a big old smile and called him his friend. So what did everyone get out of this? Was this meeting a win, guys? And if so, for whom? David, you want to go first?

David French: Well, sometimes me and the boys just kind of get together, Michelle. That’s what it felt like, quite honestly, that he sort of sees that Xi and Putin are his only true peers on the world stage; that the rest of the entire Western alliance, that those are his subordinates; that all of those people are just the people who do what he wants.

And that when he’s meeting with Xi and when he’s meeting with Putin, he’s meeting with the people who are at his level — the other key nuclear and military powers around the world. This fits his spheres of influence worldview very well — that we divide the world up into these various zones, and you get to control your zone, I get to control my zone.

And this is part of the root of the way he approaches the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Ukraine is to Putin what Canada is to the United States — the 51st state. And so, nothing is surprising about a summit like this. And it’s also not surprising at all that there would be no productive diplomatic breakthrough in any way, shape or form. But it is an interesting illustration of the way he sees the world, and it’s also an illustration of part of the reason he has seemed, and his administration seems, to tilt more toward Russia, incredibly, in the conflict. So, I thought this was a perfect symbol of his second term.
Cottle: Jamelle?

Jamelle Bouie: Yeah, I mean, I think that’s exactly right. The president, he has, firstly, a might-makes-right, the-strongest-always-has-the-right-to-dominate-the-weakest worldview. And this conference is — to the extent that you can call it a conference — it’s two autocrats and a would-be autocrat coming together and, like, commiserating over their various desired territorial acquisitions. I don’t know. It’s worth saying that this view — this might-makes-right, we-have-our-own-sphere-of-influence view — has not produced a world of greater stability.
French: No.

Bouie: It has done the exact opposite. Leniency, for example, toward Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is not actually going to make it less likely that a war is going to break out elsewhere. It’s going to make it more likely, right? If you establish, as the rule for international affairs, that the biggest and the strongest country gets to take what they want, then that’s what’s going to happen, and it’s not going to be a world of reduced conflict.

Cottle: So I have a question about the conference itself, and I like your “if we could even call it a conference” remark, because some people dubbed this summit Yalta 2.0, which is a reference to the 1945 meeting, where the soon-to-be World War II victors were meeting to essentially discuss the fate of Europe and divvy up the world. But Yalta lasted days and was coming at the end of this monumental war.

This was, like, an hour: You stop by, you smile for the photos, and then you move on. I can’t imagine that anything productive could have even begun to be discussed. But if you’re Putin and what you’re looking for is legitimacy on the world stage and have a signal sent that you’re back in the fold of sorts or whatever, it seems like, from a P.R. perspective, this actually could be very useful to Putin but not really so much to Trump. I mean, has Trump once again been used on some level?

French: I think there’s very little question that he’s been used here, and there’s very little question this is helpful to Putin; just as there’s very little question that when Trump tried to strike the diesel deal before the midterms, that was also very helpful to Putin. There’s been thing after item after item after thing after item that has demonstrated, in essence, that Trump is essentially moving America toward switching sides.

And if we think we’re being unfair about might makes right, let’s remember that just in the last week or so, we’ve seen Marco Rubio say — and Pete Hegseth really amplify it — this old Roman quote: “Stop quoting laws to men with swords,” which, I can think of few better formulations of “might makes right.”

I mean, that’s saying “might makes right” without using exactly those words. But it is perfectly illustrative of the worldview that Hegseth has of his use of the military; that Trump has of the United States on the world stage. And increasingly, I don’t know why so many Republicans are latching onto Marco Rubio as the last great reasonable hope for Republicans. No, this is a guy who’s cast his lot. He’s all in. So this is a “might makes right” administration. This very chummy meeting with these two great powers is very consistent with that.
Cottle: Jamelle, do you want to throw something in?

Bouie: I have basically two thoughts that relate to the various history references we’ve made so far. The first is just the comparison to the Yalta Conference. There’s a certain art to making historical analogies, right? You’ve got to take seriously what you’re comparing it to. And as mentioned, Yalta comes at the end of the Second World War. And part of what makes Yalta, in the American view, often considered a great tragedy was that the goal was not divvying up Europe for spheres of influence but how do we have European self-determination, right?

Like, how do we restore something like self-government in Europe? And what happens is, Stalin takes this as an opportunity to actually expand the Soviet sphere of influence and, in particular, gobble up Poland again. So, because Churchill and Roosevelt are there, kind of like, “How do we protect free Europe?” And Stalin has these ulterior motives. I’m not sure it’s, like, the best analogy. What’s a better analogy is the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885, when European colonial powers divvied up Africa as part of their spheres of influence, right? So kind of deciding we’re going to colonize Africa, and here’s who gets what. That, to me, is a much better analogy for thinking about how Trump views the world and how he views his peers — who he views as his peers.
Cottle: You just need a pithier title for that. Yalta 2.0 versus ——
Bouie: Yeah. Yalta sounds better, but ——
Cottle: It does sound good.
Bouie: But it’s more late-stage European colonialism. The other thing ——
Cottle: Sorry. Go ahead.
Bouie: —— is just, David mentioned, Hegseth and Rubio, using that phrase, “Stop quoting laws to men with swords” — it’s worth saying that comes from Plutarch’s “The Life of Pompey.”

And the translation I have up here is, “Stop quoting laws. We carry weapons,” right? It’s worth saying that Pompey helped topple the Roman Republic. He briefly co-ruled with Caesar and Crassus, and then he was eventually defeated in the civil war, assassinated and beheaded, right? They’re using the quote as if to say, “Look how mighty we are.” In the actual story that they’re taking it from, the guy who says it has a terrible end, right? Like, he’s beheaded, his head kept as a trophy by his enemies. This happens a lot with them. They’re often quoting classical references but completely obliterating the meaning of the classical reference.

There’s one I believe they’ve used before, which has a similar meaning. “The strong do what they can, and the weak suffer what they must,” which is said by the Athenians, as they are rampaging during the Peloponnesian War. And what happens is the Athenians lose that war. They lose the war and suffer immensely. So that’s all.
Cottle: I feel like they’re just going to stand up and scream for Sparta at some point. But like, Jamelle, did your dog want to get in here?
Bouie: Yeah, I think my dog wanted to get in here.
French: They love themselves some Sparta, Michelle.
Cottle: They do love them. Like, I expected to see them shirtless and running and like, it all ——
Bouie: Which again ——
Cottle: Oh, Jesus Christ.
Bouie: —— Sparta lost that war.
Cottle: That’s not what matters. It made a great movie.

Bouie: They said, “Come and take them,” and the Persians were like, “OK.” And they did. I mean, it’s so funny to me. Let me put it this way: Ancient Greek statuary, Roman statuary — we now know it was colorful, right? Like, we’ve lost the color; it’s eroded with time.
Cottle: My daughter complains about that all the time.

Bouie: What we have is the white marble. And I feel like the Hegseths and the Rubios and the far-right Twitter world, they are obsessed with the white marble and unable to see the actual history and truth and whatnot about those things.
Cottle: OK. Classical education is so important. So I want to ——
Bouie: I know, I’m like the woke one on here, but I have a Latin dictionary on my shelf behind me, like ——

Cottle: I had no doubt that you would have the Latin dictionary back there. But I want to go back now — not to take it somewhere less exalted, but: Nvidia. All this is happening about a week after Nvidia’s co-founder and C.E.O., Jensen Huang, resigned after it was revealed that he was having affairs with multiple women, one of whom, unfortunately, U.S. intelligence agencies believe to be a Chinese spy.

As you know, Trump and Jensen are buddies. Trump encouraged him, called him his friend. The president has said he would certainly not mind if Huang were reinstated. But at the same time, you’ve got the Treasury secretary out there and the commerce secretary out there, publicly feuding over the response to this and how to restrict China’s access to Nvidia’s A.I. chips. What do you make of all of this happening at this moment? And where do you see it going?

French: You know, I think it’s perfectly symbolic of Trump’s second term, to be frank. You have the stink of corruption. Here you have Trump massively increasing his stake in Nvidia over the course of his second term. You have Jensen Huang, supposedly — and, with no doubt — an absolutely brilliant man but also demonstrating that brilliance and wisdom are not the same things, that brilliance and morality are not the same things. And so, what happens? He gets brought low by the thing that has brought men low, prideful men low, over the course of millennia.

And then you have this weird spasm of tech bros rallying to the Jensen Huang flag, where you’re sort of demonstrating the way in which a lot of these tech lords seem to think that ordinary rules of human conduct don’t quite apply to them — because he’s just so key, in this entire A.I. phenomenon.
Cottle: He’s so special.

French: He’s God’s special snowflake here. And then, you have one of the fundamental paradoxes of the time. This idea that, OK, A.I. will kill us, but we can’t stop its development at all because China might race ahead of us, and I guess their A.I. will kill us before our A.I. will kill us. What’s the contest here? And so, we’re really afraid of China, but oh, by the way, we’re going to defend a guy who seemed to have created a multibillion-dollar conduit for some of our most advanced chips to perhaps fall into the hands of the Chinese government and perhaps even the Chinese military.

So all of this is, I think, Michelle, so symbolic of the problems that we have with this current generation of tech lords and with the entire A.I. conversation. It is a terrifying and also promising technology that has been created by men and women of undeniable intellect and undeniable, incredible intellectual horsepower but of extremely dubious wisdom and morality.
French: Extremely dubious. And maybe I’m being — I think I’m being too charitable for Jamelle.
Cottle: I feel that’s a good understatement.

Bouie: Yeah, no. I would say that’s a very generous way of describing these people. I would say that just because you can do math well doesn’t mean you’re not an idiot. And that’s generally how I feel about a lot of these people. Really, just the arrogance, right? The arrogance, lack of any kind of sense of humility or broader social responsibility. A sense that they are the masters of the world. I mean, one of the interesting things about this entire thing is that marital infidelity — bad. Marital infidelity and then ——
Cottle: With a Chinese spy?

Bouie: But like not uncommon, right? So it’s sort of like, OK, if it were just that. If it were just that he was cheating on his wife, OK. Not great, but I’m not sure they’re going to remove a C.E.O. for that. But with a Chinese spy and not — like, an obvious Chinese spy, right? Like, there is a great “S.N.L.” bit about this, and it was like: You should assume that this person is trying to steal secrets from you. What are you thinking? But now that he’s been removed, you see other, like, Silicon Valley, tech A.I. titans try to close ranks around him. Just be like: Oh, you’ve got to reappoint this guy. Elon’s like: He’s so important.

The next Congress should look at that — look at the way they’re trying to close ranks around him — and be like, “These people need to be held accountable in serious ways.” If this is their reaction to what really is a critical violation of American national security, we cannot trust them with anything.

Cottle: All right, Jamelle, that tees us up. We’re going to pivot to the next Congress. What we’re seeing: We got the Democrats rolling in. In the House, they’ve teed up to have Hakeem Jeffries as the next speaker — a historic first Black speaker for the country. On the Senate side, we’re seeing a little more friction. We’ve got Senator Chuck Schumer, the Democratic leader, being challenged for his post by Senator Chris Van Hollen. Now, Schumer just led his team to a massive electoral win, but there are a lot of Democrats, including some senators, who are really, really eager for new blood in leadership. So, guys: Thoughts and feelings about Schumer’s future? Jamelle, you want to go first?

Bouie: Sure. I think I’ve said this before on this podcast of ours. I don’t think that Chuck Schumer is a wartime consigliere, you know? I just don’t think he’s right for the moment. And so, I’m glad to see this leadership challenge by Chris Van Hollen, if nothing else, as an expression of the very real discontent that exists for Schumer among at least — I’m not going to say the Democratic base. I will say the small but significant cohort of people who pay close attention to Democratic politics and have opinions about all this stuff. So I’m glad to see the challenge.

I will say, I’m not sure it’s going to succeed, for, I think, reasons that are pretty straightforward. The first is that Democrats picked up nine Senate seats. It’s very hard to wage a campaign against someone who can claim that in their pocket. The other thing is, as much as I have a lot of very serious criticisms of Schumer, especially his orientation toward the administration in the first few months, since then, he’s been a pretty effective minority leader.

Part of the reason this previous, or the soon-to-be previous, Congress was so unproductive was because the administration had no real legislative program. The Republicans in Congress had no particular interest in legislation. But also, what legislation they did want to pass, basically Senate Democrats kept it from ever coming to the floor. And they’ve also been real obstacles to the administration’s attempt to confirm judges and executive branch officials, who are too far gone, right? And so, I don’t expect the challenge to succeed, because I think that, from the perspective of the members, Schumer has been perfectly fine.

Cottle: Yeah. I’ve been interested. This happens. I listen to all these people talk about, “Well, do you think they’re going to succeed in getting somebody else in there besides Jeffries?” And I’m like, “Are you high? Really?” The man just engineered a huge win with his team. They’re not going to replace Jeffries. I mean, I guess there’s a slight chance that they’re going to throw Schumer overboard. I’d like to defend him for just a second, along the same lines of what you’re talking about. I mean, he went out there and recruited candidates that were the best candidates in many places for this.

Yes, he had some stumbles. Janet Mills was not a great choice in Maine, but you know what? Graham Platner wasn’t, either, so let’s not get too spun up about that. And I have been talking to Schumer, literally for months and months, about the Southern strategy he had in mind for turning out Black voters in the South and making inroads. And at the time, I remember thinking, “Oh, yeah, right, pull the other one. That’s going to work.” But don’t I look like a jerk? So he is not necessarily a wartime consigliere, but now I want to just say that it’s time for him to be talking about succession. I know they don’t like to say what they’re going to do, because then they’re lame ducks or whatever, but the party wants and needs some fresh faces, some fresh blood in there.

He’s up for re-election in a couple years. He really needs to do a little bit of what Nancy Pelosi did when she was under fire. Pelosi turned into this great icon, and everybody loved her, and she stuck it to Trump all the time, but she also faced a couple of coup attempts because people thought that the conference needed to have fresh blood. And I think that she wound up saying: OK, I’ll serve for x more years, and then I’ll step aside from leadership.

And that was how they ended that uprising. I think Schumer is in a position where he needs to do something similar and just make clear to his people that he understands that he needs to be planning for this. But you know, that’s just me. David, did you have anything you wanted to throw in?

French: I’ve kind of done a little bit of a 180 on this, to be honest. So just from the standpoint of “Should Schumer leave?” — all other things being equal, absolutely not. It’s like saying that Mike Brown should step down after “Knicks in five.” But then I took a second look at it, thinking about it overnight, and Schumer is — what? — 75 years old. And I do think that we need to have a pattern and establish a pattern and practice of people — even if they feel vigorous, even if they feel like they’ve got a lot left to give — of starting to step back, because it has been a massive problem. This rule by people who will not let go has been a massive ——
Cottle: Just cling to those offices.

French: So it strikes me, to continue with the sports analogy, how much better would it have been if Jordan stopped after the shot in ’98 and had not had the Washington Wizards interlude after that? No, quit on a high point, not as senator — Schumer is still senator, right? And then show the way. Show how it is done that you can hand over the baton, that you can have a reasonable and orderly succession.

Cottle: So one of the things that these leaders are going to be expected to do is balance the legislative mandate in terms of pushing policy goals with the accountability mandate, which I know we’re all looking forward to.

The House Oversight chairman, Robert Garcia, has been making the rounds, talking about what he’s focusing on and what other committees are going to be focusing on. So they’re coming out swinging. Recently, Garcia sent out — to over a dozen members of Trump’s inner circle — letters, asking them to preserve documents in case they were going to need them in future investigations. This list included Trump’s two older sons, Eric and Don Jr.; son-in-law Jared Kushner; chief of staff, Stephen Miller, who’s just a little slice of evil; Vice President JD Vance.

So then last week, the White House counsel, Will Scharf, fired back with his own letter, accusing Garcia of harassing Trump and trying to score political points, and he argued that these investigations could in fact be illegal. All right, so how do the Dems run these investigations without the public viewing them as retribution or simply getting exhausted? David, put on your legal hat for us.

French: I don’t think everyone has adjusted to the new reality yet. Because the old reality was that one party would win a narrow election and then perhaps overreach or perhaps go too far — push too far too fast. I mean, this is one of the things that happened with Trump in Trump 2.0. He won by a couple of points in the popular vote, and he ran as if he were Reagan. I mean, he governed as if he were Reagan.
Cottle: It was a historic victory, David. Didn’t you know? Landslide.
Bouie: A landslide.

French: And so, he got way over his skis, just pressing on multiple fronts. And so, here come the midterms, and the midterms were a genuine landslide. I mean, they were a genuine landslide. And so, all of a sudden you’ve gone from a situation in which you’re saying, “Do we have permission to do investigations?” to “Do we have a mandate that we must do investigations?” Because the two top issues were corruption and affordability. So I would argue that this is one of those situations where if you come in and you’re not aggressive, people are going to be angry. Just as if you came in and you did nothing to try to, for example, roll back tariffs or nothing about affordability. It seems like if there is a mandate, it’s a double mandate.

One, do something about tariffs pronto, if at all humanly possible. Do something about gas prices — meaning the war — if at all possible. And then, also get after the corruption. You know, think about how long the call has gone up, “Drain the swamp, drain the swamp, drain the swamp.” That is a genuine desire of voters, and Trump swamped the swamp. I mean, he filled the swamp. And so, I think that ——
Bouie: He dredged a new swamp ——
French: He dredged ——
Cottle: All right, but you’ve got to have priorities.
French: He added the whole Everglades outside of Washington.
Cottle: So I’ve talked to members, and they’re like: Well, we can do a lot, but we can’t do it all at the same time.
French: True.
Cottle: And one of the concerns is, how do you prioritize?
French: I think you take another run at Pete Hegseth. I think you take another run at accountability, because what does this do?
Cottle: Oh, yeah.

French: What does this do? It does two things at once: It’s dealing with the war, and it’s dealing with corruption. Right there. Two things at once. Two birds with one stone. And so, I think there’s some big initiatives where you can start attacking affordability, start attacking accountability, prong all at once, and that’s not too heavy a lift.

Bouie: So on the “can’t do everything at once” with investigations. This is where maybe I might disagree with the members themselves. I think that if you are going to have a centrally directed set of investigations from Oversight and the various committees, then sure — you can’t do everything at once.

But I do think that there is maybe space to, instead of having the main committees tackle this primarily, to first create just a select committee that exists to do the big-target investigations. A select committee that’s just investigating Hegseth. A select committee that’s investigating the president, right? Your job is to begin to dig into everything we can do. A select committee on investigating DOGE — whatever. But then also, I think, this is a place where delegating more authority to subcommittees can be a fruitful way to divvy up the work and allow Congress to do more at once.

I think, within the paradigm of Congress being more centrally directed, yes, there are limits to what you can do. But if you begin to just devolve more authority to the committee and subcommittee level, you can begin to do more. You can have more people doing more things. The problem, I think, for leadership is that this is a little more unpredictable, right? You cannot have as tight a leash on everything everyone’s doing in this kind of world. And I would say that this is a risk worth taking. In the end, a Congress where members are more empowered to act autonomously is maybe a better equilibrium than one where everything is concentrated in the leadership. But that’s just ——

Cottle: I mean, my sense is that this is what they’re doing to some degree. I mean, especially in the House where Jeffries is not a heavy … he’s not a top-down sort of guy. Oversight’s doing stuff, and the Judiciary is — I think the HELP — Health, Education, Labor and Pensions — Committee is doing stuff, maybe looking at the direction of a certain head of Health and Human Services. I don’t know. But my sense is that they are divvying ——
Bouie: I don’t know what you’re talking about, Michelle.
Cottle: I don’t know. But we’re going to get so much hate mail over that. OK. Direct it all to Jamelle. I blame him.
Bouie: Direct it to me. I’m the insensitive one.

Cottle: You are. Jamelle is notoriously insensitive. So I do think that that’s kind of what they’re … but there’s just so much. I mean, there are so many things to look at. This is an incredibly corrupt period, and this administration has been an abject disgrace. I just don’t know how they’re going to keep on track. I mean, they just need a flow chart, and I don’t know.
French: Can we talk about the law for a minute?
Cottle: Oh, can we?

French: Yeah, because the impeachment — there’s a good reason I bring up impeachment as an initial effort at accountability, because that’s something where Congress really is in the most control of the process; that the administration has no ability to stymie it. But when it comes to the investigations, what you’re going to see is — and to understand what’s happening, the threats from the White House, there have also been threats from the D.O.J. that these investigations could be criminal. They sent their own “preserve your records.”

That’s completely bogus. We know there are broad congressional immunities. There is a power of inquiry in Congress that’s been laid out from the Supreme Court in a case that’s 99 years old — from 1927 — affirming the power of inquiry of Congress. But how do they enforce it? And so, that’s what you’re going to see — that what the administration is setting the stage for is large-scale resistance to these subpoenas, large-scale resistance to congressional investigations.

Will Congress be able to sue in its own right and have standing to sue to get court orders to try to compel the administration? Because if Congress does “contempt of Congress,” which it’s tried in the past in the face of recalcitrant chief executives, well, guess who prosecutes that? The Department of Justice, run by the president. So, in many ways, what we’re going to see, I think, is the Democrats trying very hard to get as much information as they possibly can, in the face of an overwhelming resistance from the administration, where the Democrats have very few levers to pull to compel compliance.

And so, you could easily see large-scale resistance followed by large-scale pardons to try to remove this from the criminal justice system. And so, I just want to highlight that because the law enforcement rests entirely in the hands of the president; Congress isn’t as potent. The entire investigative process depends more on the honor system than many Americans would like to think, except when it comes to impeachment. That the administration cannot stop.

Bouie: Just to add to that: I think what that suggests, as far as strategy goes, is that although I do think that, say, Donald Trump is deserving of an immediate impeachment trial, I do think that there is real utility in basically trying to roll up ——
Cottle: His minions?

Bouie: —— high-level officials, like minions, right? Hegseth is sort of the perfect first target, but Russell Vought, who has been engaged in basically a conspiracy to rob Congress of its power over the purse, right? There are all these people within the administration who, I think, are ripe targets for impeachment proceedings. And although cabinet impeachments are very rare — there have basically been two in American history — I still think they are easier lifts, right?
Cottle: Yeah, that’s true.

Bouie: I’m not sure if you could get 11 Republican votes to remove Hegseth. Maybe you could. I think it’s worth trying. I think it’s worth a shot. But targeting the minions for impeachment, in addition to those, can be investigations of their own accord, right? And you can have a very public set of hearings about what’s going on in C.B.O. [Congressional Budget Office], what’s going on in the Defense. And one thing I think — it’s just interesting to think about is — we have, all of a sudden, a bunch of new Democratic attorneys general. I do wonder, to the extent that investigations uncover violations of state law, what happens there?

Cottle: You’ve got to love the state offices. I’m always beating that drum. Do we think that, in the midst of all this, there’s any chance that, I don’t know, Congress might want to look into whatever caused the entire nation to seemingly melt down in the last week? Microsoft, banking tech, airlines, N.S.A.’s internal comms network or Apple services. I mean, people are very anxious about this, and is there anything to be done, or is this just one of those things we’re going to have to get used to?

Bouie: I mean, the White House basically gutted the entire federal bureaucracy, including people whose job it is to monitor stuff like this. So I think we should expect more of it. But also, it’s a reminder, I think, to everyone that yes, who runs the government matters and the decidedly unsexy and slow stuff of maintenance and improvement is critical.
Cottle: So sexy. Love it. David, do you want to throw anything in before ——

French: Yeah, you’re not just electing, and I think this is something that happened particularly on the right, when character became utterly devalued as a concept. They began to look at it as, “Well, we’re just electing, don’t get mad at me, I’m just interested in policy.” And they started to elect people as if they’re, like, Policy Bot 9,000. They just are going to come in, and they’re going to spit out my favorite policies, when actually governing a country requires a lot of expertise.

It requires a lot of competence. It requires being able to be adaptable and flexible in the face of unforeseen emergencies. And when all of this is coming to pieces, who’s running to the cameras is a guy who got his start on MTV. Sean Duffy is the head of the Department of Transportation. You’ve got Markwayne Mullin, who just perpetually seems as if he’s way in and way over his head, doesn’t fully seem to understand the issues, but he’s very keen on saying it’s S.I. and not A.I. He’s very good at the style guide.
And so, people are just being reminded that competence matters, character matters.
Cottle: OK, on that upbeat note ——

Bouie: I just want to say real quick that it is a testament to the poor character of the people in power right now that no one has resigned over this. You’re telling me that civilian aviation in the U.S. was shut down and Sean Duffy hasn’t tendered his resignation? I mean, seriously, like even if it’s not his fault, right? Taking responsibility for something like this would mean saying: “I don’t know if I’m equipped to do this job. We have to find someone who can do it.” A level of self-awareness of what a disaster this was. And this inability to just take responsibility for a job you chose to take. So that comes with, yes, perks and privileges. It also comes with obligations and responsibilities. And the extent to which ——
Cottle: Oh, I love the fact that you think responsibility is still a character trait of anybody in this administration. That is so ——

Bouie: This is where I begin to sound like David. Responsibility and obligation, these things matter, and it’s just completely absent from the top leadership of the federal government. And it puts it all at risk.

Cottle: Now that Jamelle and David have essentially become the same person, on this point, we’re going to leave it there, and we’re going to go to my favorite part of the show: recommendations. What’ve you got for me? David, go low.

French: Oh, yes, Michelle, I’ve got you. Some people might think that I would be recommending this new video game, Grand Theft Auto VI, that was glowingly reviewed in The New York Times, a sprawling, like you become a … I’ve never played G.T.A., but you become a criminal in a Miami-centered place called Vice City. Nope, nope. But I do have a video game recommendation, Michelle. Your enthusiasm is just leaking through. World of Warcraft: Forever ——
Cottle: I am here for you, David.
French: Yes. So this is the revival of a game that’s about 20 years old, and it’s called World of Warcraft. It’s kind of continued on ——
Cottle: Oh, I know that.
French: I played it forever. I don’t like to brag, but I was a healing-class leader for a raiding guild in World of Warcraft.
Cottle: God, you were just covered in women, I bet. Oh, my God. Continue. Sorry.
French: I keep that quiet, because I don’t want to let loose that ——
Cottle: Start a riot.

French: Yes. And so, this is a revival of the original game. And for a lot of us who played it for a long time, it’s like a family reunion as we’re all getting the gangs back together again from 15 years ago, 20 years ago. And it’s a ton of fun, and I’m going to guarantee you — I’m going to bet you right now that there are listeners who are playing World of Warcraft: Forever, and if you are, hit me up. Send me a note. I’m Ricky Bobby, human mage. I am.
Cottle: You’re not!
French: I’m Ricky Bobby, the human mage.
Cottle: You did not get the “Talladega Nights” reference in there.
French: Absolutely. So it’s just fantastic. It’s all the nostalgia with new updates. It’s a ton of fun.

Bouie: A few weeks ago, I rewatched “Saving Private Ryan” for the first time in a long time, and it occurred to me — well, a friend sort of said, “Oh, you got to watch ‘Band of Brothers.’ You should rewatch that as well.” And I was like, “I don’t think I’ve ever watched ‘Band of Brothers’ all the way through.” So over the past week, I have watched “Band of Brothers” all the way through, and I have to say, I think it might be the single best thing HBO has ever produced. It is a ——
Cottle: Oh, that’s a bold statement.

Bouie: No, I really think this is true. It’s a remarkable piece of fiction. There is, as always, a critique to make about the kind of greatest generation mythmaking that I think “Band of Brothers” is a part of, that “Saving Private Ryan” is a part of.

I’ll recommend, as part of this, a great book called “Half American,” by Matthew F. Delmont. The subtitle of the book is “The Epic Story of African Americans Fighting World War II at Home and Abroad.” And so, it’s a book about the Black experience of the war, both in the European and Pacific theaters and at the home front. And the late ’90s, early 2000s greatest generation mythmaking basically doesn’t even touch that whatsoever. And I, speaking as someone who’s, like, related to veterans, it’s something that does bother me. But that kind of bracketed “Band of Brothers” — a remarkable piece of television. Highly recommend it.
Cottle: I just want to note that even when you’re recommending mainstream HBO fare, you managed to work a highbrow book in there. So way to be on brand, Jamelle. I’m just saying.

I’m going in a completely different direction, and I’m going to recommend a 26-year-old Polish guitar phenom, goes mononymously by the name Marcin. And he specializes in percussive fingerstyle, but he takes that place, he combines it with electric and modern, and he does this classical stuff. He does things with a guitar that no human being should be able to do.

He just dropped a new video last week. It’s called “Panic Attack.” He’s got a new album coming out next year. He’s been on tour, but he’s only touring in Europe. So for those looking for a Christmas present for me, I would like — I think that would be great — some tickets for that. But check it out. You can find it, obviously, streaming online. Marcin. OK. And with that, we are going to land this plane. Guys, it’s been magic!
French: Michelle, your transition from Tennessee girl to The New York Times elite is now complete.
Cottle: Don’t you mock me. I’m not taking any guff from you. You just go play your video games. I’m not taking any abuse from either of you. Thank you, though. Thank you for coming to play.
Bouie: Always happy to do it.
French: Thanks Michelle.
